patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Darnell Washington is a 62-year-old right-handed African American man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia who presents to the emergency department after acute onset of right-sided weakness. He was in his usual state of health earlier this morning, watching television with his wife, when at approximately 09:45 he noted sudden-onset weakness of his right hand — he dropped his coffee mug when he tried to grip it. He immediately noticed that his right leg also felt heavy when he stood up, and his wife observed a subtle droop of the right side of his face. She called 911 without delay. EMS arrived at 09:57 and documented right facial droop, right arm and leg weakness, and a Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale score of 2. The patient's speech was noted to be entirely normal by EMS personnel. Fingerstick glucose in the field was 168 mg/dL. He was transported emergently and arrived in the emergency department at 10:18, approximately 33 minutes after symptom onset, well within the IV thrombolysis window. The patient denies any headache, nausea, vomiting, vision changes, double vision, slurred speech, dizziness, loss of consciousness, or prior similar episodes. He reports no sensation of numbness or tingling in any limb — the deficit is purely weakness. He is able to speak clearly and is not confused. His wife confirms he was entirely at his baseline at 09:30. He has no history of prior stroke, TIA, seizure, or cardiac arrhythmia. He takes his antihypertensive and diabetic medications regularly but acknowledges his blood pressure has been elevated on home monitoring for the past several weeks. He denies any recent surgery, trauma, or anticoagulant use beyond his daily aspirin.

results.title: 2019 AHA/ASA Guidelines for Early Management of Patients with Acute Ischemic Stroke
results.authors: Powers WJ, Rabinstein AA, et al.
results.key_finding: IV alteplase (0.9 mg/kg) should be administered to eligible patients within 4.5 hours of symptom onset regardless of stroke mechanism, including lacunar stroke, provided NIHSS deficits are disabling.

results.title: Classification of subtype of acute ischemic stroke: definitions for use in a multicenter clinical trial (TOAST)
results.key_finding: Small-vessel occlusion (lacunar) subtype defined by a clinical lacunar syndrome without cortical signs, maximum diameter <15 mm, and no large vessel or cardiac source identified after appropriate workup.

results.title: Guidelines for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients with Stroke and TIA (AHA/ASA 2014)
results.key_finding: For small-vessel (lacunar) ischemic stroke, intensive blood pressure control targeting systolic BP <130 mmHg and high-intensity statin therapy are recommended to reduce recurrence risk.

output.summary: Lacunar strokes represent approximately 25% of all ischemic strokes and result from occlusion of small perforating arteries supplying deep brain structures. The TOAST small-vessel occlusion subtype is characterized by a clinical lacunar syndrome (pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, ataxic hemiparesis, or dysarthria-clumsy hand), a deep subcortical lesion less than 15 mm, and the absence of a large-vessel or cardiac source. IV alteplase is indicated in eligible patients within 4.5 hours regardless of mechanism including lacunar etiology, provided deficits are functionally disabling. Secondary prevention emphasizes aggressive blood pressure reduction (target SBP <130 mmHg) and antiplatelet therapy; intensive statin and glycemic control reduce long-term small-vessel disease progression.

output.proposed: IV alteplase (tPA) 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg) for acute ischemic stroke
interactions: Aspirin 81 mg daily: antiplatelet therapy is not a contraindication to IV alteplase per AHA/ASA guidelines. Hold aspirin and other antiplatelet/anticoagulant agents for 24 hours after alteplase administration.
Metformin: no direct interaction with alteplase. Hold metformin if iodinated contrast imaging is administered; resume 48 hours after contrast if renal function remains stable.
Glipizide (sulfonylurea): no direct interaction with alteplase. Monitor blood glucose closely during and after alteplase infusion; hypoglycemia may mimic or complicate stroke.
Lisinopril (ACE inhibitor): no direct pharmacokinetic interaction with alteplase. Monitor for angioedema, a rare but recognized complication of alteplase in patients on ACE inhibitors.
Atorvastatin: no interaction with alteplase. Continue statin therapy.
contraindications: No absolute contraindications identified: INR 1.0 (not anticoagulated), platelets 231 (>100,000), glucose 188 mg/dL (acceptable range 50-400), no recent surgery or major trauma, no prior intracranial hemorrhage, blood pressure 172/96 mmHg (must be reduced to <185/110 mmHg before alteplase initiation), symptom onset 33 minutes ago (well within 4.5-hour window).

Relative consideration: NIHSS 5 with disabling deficit (inability to grip, ambulate independently) qualifies as functionally disabling; tPA eligibility should not be withheld based on low NIHSS alone if deficits are disabling per AHA/ASA 2019 guidelines.

sequence_constraints.reason: Review NCCT for hemorrhage while evaluating thrombolytic eligibility; routine laboratory, ECG, MRI and advanced imaging must not delay reperfusion.

critical_actions: Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision
Recognize that a normal initial CT does not exclude acute lacunar stroke — DWI MRI is required to confirm the diagnosis

Assess tPA eligibility: functionally disabling deficit (unable to grip independently or ambulate safely) qualifies even with NIHSS 5 — do not withhold tPA assessment for a low NIHSS if deficits are disabling
Achieve door-to-needle time <60 minutes; symptom onset is known and well within the 4.5-hour window
Confirm sinus rhythm on ECG to support non-cardioembolic mechanism
Reduce blood pressure to <185/110 mmHg before tPA administration; monitor on ACE inhibitor for angioedema
Classify mechanism as TOAST small-vessel occlusion after excluding large-vessel and cardioembolic sources

Initiate aggressive vascular risk factor secondary prevention: intensive blood pressure reduction (target SBP <130 mmHg), high-intensity statin, and tighter glycemic control (HbA1c 8.4% requires optimization)
contraindicated_actions: Do not exclude acute ischemic stroke on the basis of a normal non-contrast CT alone — a normal CT is expected in acute lacunar stroke and does not rule out the diagnosis
Do not withhold consideration of IV tPA solely because the NIHSS is low (5) — if the deficit is functionally disabling (impaired grip, unable to ambulate safely), tPA eligibility must be assessed
Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not assume small-vessel mechanism without completing cardiac monitoring and vessel imaging to exclude competing etiologies
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase outside the tPA window — risks worsening perfusion to the ischemic penumbra
key_reasoning_points: The hallmark of a lacunar (small-vessel) stroke is a pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, ataxic hemiparesis, or dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome WITHOUT cortical signs — the absence of aphasia, neglect, gaze deviation, and visual field cut is diagnostically important and points away from a cortical MCA mechanism

Left internal capsule posterior limb lacune causes contralateral (right) pure motor face, arm, and leg weakness in equal proportion — the corticospinal tract is tightly bundled here, producing this classic equi-proportionate deficit

Acute lacunar infarcts are often invisible on non-contrast CT in the first hours; a normal CT does not exclude the diagnosis and must be followed by DWI MRI, which is the confirmatory test for small deep infarcts
A modest NIHSS score may underestimate functional disability in lacunar stroke — an inability to grip or ambulate independently is disabling and qualifies for IV tPA consideration
TOAST small-vessel occlusion requires excluding both large-vessel disease (CTA/carotid duplex) and a cardiac embolic source (ECG, echo, cardiac monitoring) before the lacunar mechanism is assigned

Secondary prevention of small-vessel stroke is driven by aggressive control of vascular risk factors — blood pressure is the most important modifiable risk factor, with a target SBP <130 mmHg; diabetes control (HbA1c) and high-intensity statin therapy are also critical
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Non-contrast CT is the required first-line study in the acute window; MRI adds tissue-based selection and is not mandatory for the diagnosis.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC/coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG/troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA/CTP do not wait for creatinine.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward — classic pure motor lacunar syndrome from left posterior limb of internal capsule lacune. Clear TOAST small-vessel mechanism once cortical signs are recognized as absent. Red herrings: normal initial CT and modest NIHSS. DWI confirms the diagnosis.
clinical_pearls: Pure motor hemiparesis with right face, arm, and leg in equal proportion and NO cortical signs is the textbook presentation of a left internal capsule lacunar stroke
Lacunar infarcts are often not visible on acute non-contrast CT — DWI MRI is the imaging gold standard for diagnosis
A low NIHSS does not preclude tPA eligibility if the motor deficit is functionally disabling
TOAST small-vessel occlusion requires active exclusion of both large-vessel and cardiac sources before the mechanism is assigned

case_body_concerns: Mock server single-slot limitation for order_ct_scan: this case uses two order_ct_scan calls (non-contrast as initial_tool_outputs.ct, and CTA as followup_outputs[0]). The non-contrast CT is pre-loaded as the primary initial output. The CTA follow-up is stored as the first followup_outputs entry triggered by 'request_ct_angiography'. Agents ordering CTA after non-contrast CT will correctly receive the CTA followup. Agents calling order_ct_scan a second time in a generic way may receive the same non-contrast CT from the slot — this is a known mock-server limitation documented in CLINICIAN_REVIEW_FLAGS.md.
